newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen opening higher after record close.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen opening higher after record close.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open higher after Wednesday's record close on the Dow although analysts said that a slew of data due out ahead of the opening bell could influence the market.
In addition to the September housing starts, industrial production and capacity utilization, the market will also be prey to the tide of third quarter earnings.
"I predict we will be firm at the opening. Then we have to watch the numbers," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities.
"These are fairly predictable numbers," Wachtel said, adding that the market was hoping for further evidence of an economy which was, on the whole, soft.

September housing starts are expected to drop while industrial production is expected to rise by 0.1 percent and capacity utilization is forecast at 83.3 percent, below the 85 percent level which indicates full capacity.
"Ultimately, the question is how will the numbers affect the bond market," he said, adding that any sign of strength in the economy will be taken as a negative by markets.

"Anything that smacks of good news will hurt bonds," Wachtel said. "What happens if capacity utilization inches toward that 85 percent number. Full capacity is sometimes a trigger for tightening by the Federal Reserve.

Among the companies which reported earnings this morning, McDonnell Douglas Corp reported third quarter net of $0.90, including a $0.04 charge, compared $0.85 a year ago, including a $0.11 gain. The First Call estimate was $0.91.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was up 27 points at 21,424.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 14 at 4038.
Among U.S. shares traded in London were cautious ahead of the release of this morning's economic data.
The dollar failed to advance on the yen in Tokyo and and was firm in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were modestly higher, with the long bond up 3/32 to yield 6.85 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that most of the country's money managers are having a good year. Stocks picked by the average manager were up an average of 14.7 percent through September 30, outpacing the 13.4 percent return on the benchmark Standard & Poor's 500 index, according to Thomson Investment Software, a Boston unit of Thomson in Toronto, the newspaper said.
The New York Times Market Place writes that Pharmaceutical stocks are on a roll for the third consecutive year, propelled by new products and renewed pricing power.
